cells.tense: Something arrives with no clear shape yet, and you are meeting it with fresh eyes right where you are.
cells.ask: Bring one unfinished thing to someone you're close to and stay in the room while it's still open. Don't present it finished — let it take the shape it takes with them.
cells.core: You can be close to someone and still be meeting them for the first time. Nothing has to be settled before you're in the room with it. You take a half-formed thing — a feeling about someone, a plan without edges — and open it with them instead of waiting until you understand it. That's why people tell you things. You're not standing outside their moment deciding how you feel about it; you're in it, with them, and that gives the moment a place to land.\n\nWhat keeps this when it's working is not more feeling. It's direction chosen from genuine engagement, once you've let something in. The care has somewhere to go afterward. Pick one half-formed thing that's been sitting in you this week and open it out loud with the person it touches. The shape might change once it's between you. That's allowed.
cells.sheetLine: You meet what has no shape yet, close and fresh.

cells.tense: You have already imagined how this will go far ahead of anything that has happened yet.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you're sure you know where it's heading. Say to the person involved that you don't know how it'll land.
cells.core: You're trying to feel your way to the end before the thing has started. Someone mentions something and you've already gone a month ahead: how they'll take it, how it'll go wrong, how you'll mend it. You're not cold, ever — you're with them at full volume. The imagining has simply outrun what's here, and the warmest thing you could do is to stop at what's in front of you.\n\nThis isn't a lack of care. It's care with nowhere to land yet. What helps is care that doesn't exhaust itself — holding space without gripping it. Pick one thing you're sure you know the shape of, and say out loud to the person involved that you don't know how it will land. Then let the evening be ordinary, and see how much of the ahead-of-time was real.
cells.sheetLine: You're feeling the whole arc before it can start.

cells.tense: You are still standing at a door that closed, and the door is behind you now.
cells.ask: Say one true, concrete thing to one person today about what meeting them again is actually like for you. Truth only, no display.
cells.core: There aren't many moments now where you and someone meet without knowing each other already. Openness with another person used to be ordinary, and it isn't lately. What's absent isn't closeness — it's the beginner's ground to be close on, the willingness to be felt without already having the outcome. What you already sense about people is usually right, and it doesn't have to be held behind glass.\n\nDon't push warmth at close range to fix this. Take it a step back instead: use what you already notice about someone, and let one observation out where they can hear it. The line you haven't said to one person — say it today, plainly. What you already see has something to stand on; that's what lets meeting happen.
cells.sheetLine: You can still feel, but meeting someone is behind glass.

cells.tense: You are already coloring how a conversation with someone close lands, and you are calling it just taking it in.
cells.ask: Pick one moment today when someone near you shifts and you went along with it. Afterward, write one plain line: 'I moved when that happened.'
cells.core: You're already reading a room before anyone says a word — their mood, what they're not saying, what they need next. The skill is running whenever you're with someone, and what gets said instead is 'that's just what they're like' — as if the read were coming from them and not from you.\n\nThis isn't a fight with your instincts. It's about keeping your own hands on what's actually unfolded in front of you: the sentence they did say, the thing you actually saw, the step you actually took. Name that one moment — the moment, then your own line. The point of noticing is to keep it yours.
cells.sheetLine: You read people closely and call it just noticing.

attempts.check: The cells call the ability in question imagination, but the record's generator is the card: learning, exploring feeling with fresh sensitivity and wonder. Nothing in the record says the person likes surprises or has a talent for invention, and a reader who is engaged by what is actually there could reasonably say so; the profile survives because it is carried by what they open to and how they take it in. The asks survive a misread because each one aims at the partner's own act, not at a promised outcome. The sentence that serves the writer is around training the eye and staying far back — it sounds like wisdom and says nothing anyone could use.
